Posidoniaceae is a family of marine plants whose native region is not specified in the supplied source. Its members have flattened stems and narrow leaves, with small flowers containing both male and female parts gathered in spongy clusters.

Hyparrhenia is a genus of annual and perennial bunch grasses mostly native to tropical Africa, with some occurring in warmer parts of Eurasia, Australia and Latin America. Many are known as thatching grasses, and their flowering branches divide into twin spikes bearing paired flower clusters.

Aloe is a genus of flowering succulents native to tropical and southern Africa, Madagascar, Jordan, the Arabian Peninsula, India and islands of the Indian Ocean. Most have rosettes of thick, fleshy leaves and clusters of tubular flowers that are often yellow, orange, pink or red; some South African aloes grow as trees.
edibilityNote: Some species are edible, but many species have irritating or harmful juice or latex.

summary: Anisodontea is a genus of flowering mallows native to South Africa and Lesotho. Its members typically have toothed leaves with three or five uneven lobes, and pink to magenta flowers with streaked petals and dark anthers.

Arctotis is a genus of annual and perennial plants native to dry, stony slopes in southern Africa. Their daisy-like flowers tend to close in late afternoon or dull weather, although garden cultivars have been developed in many colours and often remain open longer.

A genus of flowering plants endemic to Macaronesia—the Canary Islands, Savage Islands and Madeira. Ornamental hybrids involving Argyranthemum species bear abundant single or double daisy-like flowers throughout summer.

A genus of aquatic plants with no explicitly stated native origin, found mainly in tropical and subtropical regions, especially the Americas. Most grow in wet conditions, spread through seeds or stem pieces, and have leaves that smell lemony when crushed.

A genus of woody climbing or scrambling flowering plants endemic to Australia. They have alternate simple leaves, flowers whose petals form a tube at the base, and fleshy berries containing many seeds.
A widespread grass genus native to many countries on every inhabited continent and many islands. Often called beardgrass, bluegrass or bluestem, some species become invasive where introduced.

A genus of annual or biennial flowering herbs native to Mediterranean regions of Europe and Asia. They have narrow simple leaves, yellowish flower clusters and seed pods that split open; C. sativa was historically cultivated as an oil plant.

A genus of mostly evergreen shrubs native to warm temperate and tropical parts of the Americas, from the southernmost United States to central Chile. Many have strongly scented flowers and are grown ornamentally, but all plant parts are toxic and can cause severe gastroenteritis if eaten.
edibilityNote: All plant parts are toxic and cause severe gastroenteritis if eaten.

summary: A genus of wildflowers native to western and central North America. Their daisy-like flower heads have curled white, blue or purple outer petals surrounding yellow centres.
A genus of woody evergreen shrubs endemic to southwestern Western Australia. Their oil-bearing leaves often smell pleasant when crushed, while the small flowers have waxy-feeling petals.

A genus of evergreen aromatic trees and shrubs with no explicitly stated native origin, distributed across tropical and subtropical Asia and Oceania. Their leaves and bark contain aromatic oils. Inner bark from several species supplies cinnamon, while C. tamala is used as Indian bay leaf.
edibilityNote: Inner bark from several species is used as cinnamon; C. tamala is used as malabathrum, tejpat or Indian bay leaf.

summary: A genus of deciduous flowering shrubs native to southern Europe, North Africa and southwest Asia. Yellow-to-orange pea-like flowers appear through summer, followed by inflated seed pods that change from pale green to red or copper.
edibilityNote: Only C. istria is documented: Bedouins of Sinai and Negev ate its seeds during scarcity; this does not establish edibility for the genus.

summary: A non-vascular hornwort recorded in the Iberian Peninsula, Oregon, the Azores and Brazil, with no native origin stated. Its body has small stalk-like tubers, while its spores turn from yellow to black as they mature. Male and female plants are separate, with females larger, and it inhabits temporarily wet bare mineral soil.

An annual liverwort distributed worldwide, with no more specific native origin stated. It usually forms complete blue-green rosettes without the red colouring seen in some related species. A pioneer of open, moist ground, it is especially common in fields and fallow fields.

An annual liverwort distributed worldwide, with no more specific native origin stated. Its blue-green to green rosettes have a distinctive deep V-shaped groove along the upper surface. It pioneers open ground that ranges from moist to seasonally dry and is especially frequent in fields and fallow fields.
A small genus of three plants in the carrot family. One member, Cyclospermum leptophyllum, is a well-known weed called marsh parsley or fir-leafed celery.

A genus of succulent plants common in southern and eastern Africa, with a few species in Madagascar, Réunion, Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Its seed capsules open when wet and close as they dry, while the leaves are often grooved or covered with bladder-like cells.
A genus of daisy-family plants native to southern Africa. Its flowers are usually bisexual, and some species can hybridize with Osteospermum to produce cultivated ornamentals.

A genus of annual or perennial marsh and bog plants whose single recognized species is native to the Americas. Plants may grow above water, bear floating leaves or become seasonally submerged, and they produce white flowers.

A genus of three dwarf evergreen shrubs found from temperate to subarctic parts of the Northern Hemisphere and in parts of the Southern Hemisphere. They form mats with small needle-like leaves and bear fairly dry, edible berries.
edibilityNote: The genus bears edible fruit.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native to the Mediterranean region, western and Central Asia, and China. It includes the leafy vegetable called rocket or arugula, and its members have deeply lobed leaves and creamy-white flowers with purple veins.
edibilityNote: The genus includes the leaf vegetable rocket, also called arugula.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native from the southwestern United States to northwestern Mexico.

A small genus of herbaceous annuals native to warm parts of the southern United States, Mexico, the Caribbean and northern South America. They have bluish-green, slightly succulent leaves and large, funnel-shaped flowers on long stems, in colors including pink, purple, white and blue.
A genus of Mediterranean grasses comprising four described species.

A genus of herbaceous flowering plants whose species are variously native to Latin America, Australia, New Zealand, Papuasia, Hawaii, island Southeast Asia, eastern Africa and Madagascar. Leaf size varies dramatically: subgenus Panke contains giants, while others are low, mat-forming plants with small leaves. At least some species form an unusual intracellular partnership with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
edibilityNote: Stalks of some species are edible; G. tinctoria stalks are peeled and eaten fresh or prepared in salads, liquor or marmalade.

summary: A genus of flowering plants whose species are native to Eurasia, Africa, Australia and the Pacific Islands. Its annual or perennial herbs range from creeping or cushion-forming plants to upright forms, with small white or pink flowers. Some species are grown for floristry, especially baby's-breath.
edibilityNote: Some species flavor liqueur, cheese and ice cream; G. rokejeka is used to make halva.

summary: A genus of annual herbs native from southern Europe through central and southwestern Asia, and in Africa. They are frail, short-lived plants with slender roots and thin upright or rising stems, typically producing inconspicuous white to soft-pink flowers in early spring.

A genus of flowering plants native to the Mediterranean basin, western Europe, western Asia and the Caucasus. It includes annuals, evergreen perennials and low woody shrubs used ornamentally in rock gardens, beds and borders.

A genus of small bulb-forming perennials native to southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina and Uruguay. Narrow, grass-like leaves accompany honey-scented, star-shaped spring flowers, usually white or pale blue.

A genus of corm-forming plants endemic to the Cape Provinces of western South Africa. Sword-like leaves and long, wiry stems bearing star-shaped flowers make them memorable, and some species are grown as ornamentals.

A genus of flowering shrubs and trees native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. Most species have leaves divided twice into leaflets, and conspicuous large flower clusters are usually blue to purple-blue, though a few species flower white.

A genus of succulent perennial herbs native to Namibia and South Africa's Cape Provinces and Free State. They have fleshy, smooth or waxy leaves and bright yellow, orange, pink or purple flowers; their seed capsules open when wet.

A genus of evergreen shrubs and trees, mostly native to Australia, with a few occurring naturally in Malesia, seven native only to New Caledonia and one to Lord Howe Island. Many have peeling papery bark or aromatic, oil-dotted leaves, while flowers are grouped into bottlebrush-like heads or spikes.
edibilityNote: M. cajuputi oil is used in Southeast Asia to add fragrance to food.

summary: A genus of drought-adapted flowering plants native across most of Mexico and the southern United States, north to Nevada and Colorado. They grow rosettes of many long leaves; some remain stemless, while others form tall woody trunks that may branch into multiple rosettes. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants.

A genus of annual and perennial vines native to the Americas, especially Mesoamerica, with species ranging from herbaceous to woody. Five species were domesticated in pre-Columbian times for their beans, including tepary, runner, year, lima and common beans.
edibilityNote: Five species were domesticated in pre-Columbian times for their beans: tepary, runner, year, lima and common beans.

summary: A genus of free-floating aquatic ferns with a natural range mainly across tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas, Eurasia and Africa. They have no true roots; each leaf cluster has two floating green leaves and a finely divided hanging leaf that resembles a root.

A genus of flowering plants native to Africa, Europe and Asia, including both annuals and perennials. Each flower head contains many small flowers, and the remaining bracts and sepals form a memorable spiky ball after flowering.
A genus of Eurasian and North African grasses, commonly called hardgrass.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs whose native origin is not specified, although it is widely distributed across Europe, Asia, Africa and North America. Some species are fully aquatic and others grow beside water; their branching stems root at the joints, and their small white flowers form compound clusters.

A genus of large perennial grasses whose native origin is not stated in the supplied sources. Known as feather, needle or spear grasses, they are coarse plants with rolled-in leaves and branched flower clusters, occurring in grasslands and savannas.
A genus of palms native to South America. All species bear male and female flowers on the same plant, and many produce edible small palm fruits.
edibilityNote: Many species produce edible small palm fruits.

summary: A genus of mostly evergreen trees and shrubs native from Africa and Madagascar through southern Asia to the Pacific. Many have glossy foliage; a few yield rose-apple fruits eaten fresh or made into preserves, while the unopened buds of Syzygium aromaticum are the spice clove.
edibilityNote: A few species have fruits eaten fresh or preserved; unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum are used as clove spice.

summary: A genus of herbs from temperate Eurasia, occurring in central and southern Europe and southwestern Asia, with two species found only in China. It can concentrate heavy metals such as zinc and cadmium and may be useful in cleaning contaminated ground.

A genus of free-floating aquatic flowering plants with a cosmopolitan distribution, including the smallest flowering plants on Earth. They are rootless and resemble specks of cornmeal, often gathering into floating mats. They have historically been collected from water and eaten as a vegetable in Asia.
edibilityNote: Historically collected from water and eaten as a vegetable in Asia.

summary: Submerged aquatic flowering-plant genus with a worldwide temperate and tropical distribution. Its slender plants have threadlike leaves and tiny flowers, and pollination takes place underwater.

Perennial bulb-forming flowering plant native to Central Asia, northeastern Iran and the Himalayan foothills. Its strong-smelling bulb typically contains 10–20 cloves, while sulfur compounds create its pungent flavour. The cloves are eaten raw or cooked, and cooking considerably mellows and sweetens them.
edibilityNote: Cloves are eaten raw or cooked; immature leaves, flowers and scapes are also edible.

summary: Annual herb native to North Africa and West Asia. It has finely divided leaves on slender hollow stems and small white-to-yellow flowers; its leaves and seeds flavour foods as herbs and spices.
edibilityNote: Fresh or dried leaves are used as an herb, while the seeds are used as a spice.

summary: Perennial aquatic plant native to temperate and subtropical parts of Africa, Asia, Australia and the Americas. It has bright green floating leaves, small purple flowers and thick mucilage coating its underwater parts. Its young mucilage-covered stems are eaten in China and Japan, including in soups.
edibilityNote: Young mucilage-covered stems are eaten as a vegetable in China and Japan, including in regional soups.

summary: Cabbage-family flowering plant of unknown origin, including oilseed rape and the distinct rutabaga subspecies. Oilseed rape has bright yellow flowers and oil-rich seeds; low-erucic food-grade cultivars provide canola oil.
edibilityNote: Low-erucic rapeseed cultivars yield food-grade canola oil; ordinary seed naturally contains mildly toxic erucic acid.

summary: Annual flowering herb native to most of the central United States. Its flower heads are brilliant yellow with maroon or brown centres and notched petal tips. The Zuni traditionally used blossoms of the tinctoria variety for mahogany-red dye and, historically, a hot drink.
edibilityNote: The Zuni traditionally made a hot beverage from blossoms of the tinctoria variety before traders introduced coffee.

summary: Herbaceous perennial legume native to West Asia, tropical Asia, North Africa and southern Europe. Its root yields a sweet, aromatic flavouring used in confectionery and drinks, though excessive consumption can raise blood pressure and lower blood potassium.
edibilityNote: The root supplies flavouring for confectionery and beverages; dried roots are also traditionally chewed as candy.

summary: Small aquatic duckweed native to Australia and South Asia and naturalized in North America. Its form is intermediate between Lemna and Spirodela.

A bright-green herb native to parts of southern Europe and North Africa, garden parsley grows as a biennial in temperate climates but as an annual in warmer regions. Curly and flat leaves flavour and garnish food, while root parsley is eaten as a vegetable; the seeds are toxic and should be avoided.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used as herbs and garnishes, and root parsley is eaten raw or cooked; seeds are toxic and should be avoided.

summary: A palm whose native origin is uncertain after millennia of cultivation, with proposed origins including North African oases, the Persian Gulf or Fertile Crescent, and southwest Asia. It often grows as a single trunk but may form multi-stemmed clumps, and male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Female palms bear sweet, edible dates ranging from yellow or red to dark brown by variety.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit is eaten fresh or dried and used in sweet and savoury dishes.

summary: A deciduous tree of Chinese origin, though the domestic peach’s exact birthplace is unknown and East China near the Yangtze Delta is a likely candidate. Pink or red flowers usually open before the leaves, followed by juicy edible stone fruits. Smooth-skinned nectarines and fuzzy peaches are forms of the same species, despite being sold as different fruits.
edibilityNote: The juicy fruit is eaten raw; freestone types are preferred fresh and clingstones for canning.

summary: A tall annual or biennial grass cultivated for grain, ground cover and forage. Its blue-green pointed leaves and curved seed heads accompany unusual tolerance of cold and poor soil. The grain makes bread, crispbread, beer and whiskey, but ergot-infected rye can cause severe poisoning.
edibilityNote: The grain is milled for bread and fermented into beer or whiskey; ergot-infected rye can cause severe, sometimes fatal poisoning.

summary: A perennial herb or low shrub native to Arizona, California, Nevada and Oregon in the western United States, and Baja California in northwestern Mexico. Hairy branching stems carry mostly unlobed oval or lance-shaped leaves, followed from February to June by clusters of purple-blue flowers and green berries. All parts are toxic, especially unripe fruit.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially unripe fruit; poisoning may affect the heart, nervous system and digestion.

summary: A genus of deciduous trees with species native to Africa, Madagascar and Australia, baobabs comprise eight species, and genomic evidence suggests the genus originated in Madagascar. Mature trees have massive bottle-shaped or cylindrical trunks, lose their leaves in the dry season, and bear large scented flowers that open rapidly near dusk. Their large berry-like fruits hold kidney-shaped seeds in dry pulp.
edibilityNote: Fresh leaves are eaten as vegetables; dried fruit pulp from several species is used in foods, and some named species also provide edible seeds.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native from the Mediterranean basin and western Asia through the Transcaucasus and Central Asia to Pakistan. It contains 11 accepted species; several are grown for their flowers, including Virginia stock.
A flowering-plant genus in the vervain family, native entirely to the Americas. It contains 90 species, some of which have naturalised elsewhere.

A genus of fan palms native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas. Their fan-shaped leaves have bare, unarmed stalks and a midrib extending into the blade; the fruits typically turn from green to black as they mature.

A genus of flowering legumes widespread in tropical and warm-temperate regions of both hemispheres. Dense hairs often give the leaves a greyish tint, while many species contain rotenone and have historically supplied fish poison and insecticide.

A tuber-forming genus of flowering plants native exclusively to South America, with diversity centred in Chile and Brazil. Most are long-lived perennials, and their leaves twist so the undersides face upward; the colourful flowers are often flecked, striped or streaked.

A genus of columnar or tree-like cacti native to Mexico, Arizona, Central America, northern South America and the West Indies. Their ribbed green stems bear strong spines, and their funnel- or bell-shaped flowers usually open at night near the stem tips.
edibilityNote: Fruits of some species are eaten: Seri favour acidic S. gummosus fruit, and Wayuu relish S. griseus fruit.

summary: A genus of flowering monocots native to North America and northern and eastern Asia. These wetland plants spread through thick underground stems and bear inconspicuous flowers on a fleshy spike enclosed by long, narrow leaves.

An evergreen terrestrial orchid genus found from eastern and southeastern Asia to Australia and Pacific islands. Its crowded underground stems produce a few large, pleated leaves and upright sprays of open, colourful flowers in white, yellow, pink or purple.

A genus of flowering plants in the sunflower family, native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas. These rugged annuals, perennials or bushes tolerate heat and drought, producing persistent displays of cream or yellow daisy-like flower heads; three species have white rays.

A genus of spiny palms native to Central and South America and Trinidad. Their leaflets form a feather-like pattern, and species may have one stem or grow in multi-stemmed clumps; each plant bears separate male and female flowers.
edibilityNote: Fruits and seeds of several species are used as human food; the species and preparations are not specified.

summary: A genus of clump-forming flowering perennials native to Asia, especially eastern Asia. Despite their name, daylilies are not true lilies, and most species produce flowers that open in the morning and wither by night.
edibilityNote: Food use is species-specific: H. citrina flowers are used in Chinese dishes; H. fulva tubers and young leaves are eaten raw or cooked.

summary: A deciduous small tree or shrub native to the Hyrcanian forests south of the Caspian Sea in Iran. It bears aromatic golden-yellow fruit that remains hard, tart and astringent when ripe; most varieties are cooked into jams, jellies or puddings, though a few can be eaten raw.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw or processed into preserves and drinks; most varieties are too hard and tart raw. Seeds are toxic in large quantities.

summary: A genus of shrubs and vines native to tropical and warm-temperate Asia, Africa and Oceania. Its roughly 200 species may be evergreen or deciduous and are best remembered for usually fragrant white or yellow flowers, with reddish blooms rare.
edibilityNote: Some Jasminum species are used to produce teas and herbal infusions; J. sambac flowers scent green, white or sometimes oolong tea.

summary: A genus of flowering bromeliads whose species are all endemic to Brazil. Unlike most bromeliads, they grow strictly on the ground, often as flattened, star-like rosettes in Atlantic Forest leaf litter and shrubby coastal sands.

A genus of woody evergreen trees and shrubs distributed through tropical and subtropical regions worldwide; the sources do not specify whether this is its native range. Most species occur in the New World tropics, and a few bear edible fruits eaten fresh or made into jams and jellies.
edibilityNote: A few species bear edible fruit eaten fresh or made into jams and jellies.

summary: A tree native to southeast Europe and southwest Asia. Its bark flakes with age, and its yellow, juicy berries are edible only when fully ripe, aided by frost.
edibilityNote: Fruit is edible only when fully ripe, aided by frost; in Pakistan it is also consumed dried.

summary: A genus of flowering plants found mostly in southern and tropical Africa and Madagascar; the sources do not explicitly label this as its native range. Most are perennial herbs, though some are annuals, soft-wooded shrubs, succulent or tuber-based, and several species are grown ornamentally.

A perennial flowering vine native to South or possibly Southeast Asia, perhaps including India's Malabar Coast. Its fruits become peppercorns: black pepper uses cooked and dried unripe fruit, green pepper uses unripe fruit, and white pepper is the dried seed of ripe fruit. Piperine supplies the characteristic heat.
edibilityNote: Peppercorns are used as seasoning; black and green pepper come from unripe fruit, while white pepper is the dried seed of ripe fruit.

summary: A genus of flowering plants in the arum family, native to South America, Central America and southern Mexico.
A genus of liverworts with a cosmopolitan distribution; the supplied information does not specify a native origin.

A tropical genus of flowering bromeliads widespread across Mexico, Central and South America, and the West Indies. Most grow on trees, while many form water-holding tanks from tightly overlapping leaf bases; their roots mainly anchor them, and nutrients are absorbed chiefly from these reservoirs.

A genus of annual or biennial herbs originally distributed in temperate Asia. Its plants are hairless, with upright, little-branched stems and simple leaves that are often arranged in a basal rosette.

A leafy green annual, rarely biennial, native to Central and Western Asia. It has variable oval-to-triangular leaves and small green, wind-pollinated flowers, usually borne on separate male and female plants. Its leaves are commonly eaten fresh, cooked or preserved.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten fresh or cooked and may be canned, frozen or dehydrated; blanching can reduce oxalates.

summary: A genus of mostly tree-growing orchids found from Florida and the Caribbean through Mexico and the tropical Americas. Most have stiff, drought-resistant leaves and large onion-shaped storage stems, with flowers rising from the top and pollinated by bees or birds.
A genus of flowering plants in the myrtle family, native to Central and South America and the West Indies.

A genus of flowering plants native to Africa, southern Asia and Australia. Most species trail or climb, while their tubular flowers often form umbrella-like canopies or cages that temporarily trap flies during pollination.
edibilityNote: In Africa, roots and leaves of some species are eaten raw; in India, tubers are eaten raw or stewed in curries.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native mainly to rocky sites in southern Africa, with a few species elsewhere in Africa and on the Arabian Peninsula. Its daisy-like flower heads rise above fern-like foliage.
A small genus of flowering herbs and low woody plants native to the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores.
A genus of tree-growing cacti native to Central and South America. Its stems are broad and flat, and its flowers open only at night before wilting at dawn.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and resembles pitaya, though it is smaller.

summary: A genus of subshrubs, shrubs and small trees native from Mexico and the Caribbean through South America to northern Argentina. Its species typically have purple or lilac flowers that do not change colour with age, and leaves often covered with tiny scales.
A flowering-plant genus in the cucumber family, Sicyos includes species commonly called bur cucumbers.

A genus of orchids native to Mexico and Central and South America, Sobralia grows mainly on the ground in wet forests, though some plants grow on other plants. Its reed-like stems bear large, delicate flowers that open successively and may last only hours to three days.

A marine red-alga genus with a worldwide distribution, Callithamnion forms small, upright tufts of freely branching filaments. Its cells contain multiple nuclei, and most species are fertile mainly in late summer and autumn.

A red-alga genus distributed through tropical and temperate seas but absent from polar regions, Gelidium grows from tidal shores into deeper water. Its branches may be irregular or arranged in rows, and many members are used to make agar.
edibilityNote: Many Gelidium algae are used to make agar, which has food applications; gel properties vary among species, seasons and seaweed ages.

summary: A family of multicellular red algae, Corallinaceae has no native range stated in the supplied sources. Its reproductive chambers occur in distinctive clusters, separating it from the similar Sporolithaceae family.

A genus of multicellular red algae with no native range stated in the supplied sources, Lithothamnion forms crusts of closely surface-hugging filaments. It reproduces through structures containing multiple pores.

A wholly marine genus of filamentous red algae recorded from seas worldwide, Polysiphonia commonly grows on rocks, other algae, shellfish and artificial surfaces. Its usually well-branched body consists of fine filaments with a central strand surrounded by cells whose number helps identify species.

A fern species native to eastern North America, Woodwardia areolata favours moist, sandy, acidic soils. Its net-like veins, lobed fronds and marked difference between fertile and sterile fronds distinguish it, though it can be confused with the sensitive fern.

A genus of perennial plants endemic to southwestern Western Australia, Anigozanthos often survives dry spells through short underground stems, with some species dying back in summer and returning in autumn. Its velvety, brightly coloured tubular flowers resemble kangaroo paws and open into six-part fans.

An evergreen conifer tree native to parts of western North America, Picea pungens has a conical crown when young that becomes more open and irregular with age. Its stiff, sharply pointed needles range from green to pale white and are often strikingly blue-green because of surface wax.
A genus of flowering succulents, shrubs and trees, most of whose species are native to the Americas. They produce separate male and female flowers and contain highly toxic compounds.
edibilityNote: A selectively bred J. curcas variant yields an edible byproduct; its seeds are sometimes eaten roasted, but untreated seeds can be fatal.

summary: A perennial climbing vine native to East Asia. It bears cinnamon-scented flowers and rounded bulbils that can start new plants; its tubers are edible raw, unlike those of most yams.
edibilityNote: Tubers are eaten peeled, raw and grated or sliced; a vinegar-water soak is used to neutralize irritant crystals in the skin.

summary: A genus of bulb-growing perennial herbs distributed mainly in southern and eastern Africa, with some species in northern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Their fleshy leaves release a slippery juice, inspiring the name slime lilies, and some species have night-scented flowers.
A genus of bulbous perennial plants usually found in Namibia and South Africa. Most have a dormant period but grow new roots every year.

A genus of annuals, perennials and small woody plants native to sandy coasts or disturbed ground in South Africa. Their flowers have two lips: the upper has four lobes and the lower has two, while many cultivated hybrids are popular bedding plants.

A genus of perennial herbs in the ginger family native to Southeast Asia, southern China, the Indian subcontinent, New Guinea and northern Australia. They produce edible yellow or orange underground stems that are powdered to make the spice curcuma.
edibilityNote: The genus produces edible yellow or orange rhizomes, which are ground into the spice called curcuma.

summary: A genus of plants native to southern Africa. Some species are widely cultivated as ornamentals.

A perennial herb native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Its branched, aromatic yellow-to-orange underground stems are used fresh or boiled, dried and ground into a deep orange-yellow spice for colouring and flavouring, especially in curries.
edibilityNote: Rhizomes are used fresh or are boiled, dried and ground as a spice and food colouring.

summary: A genus of flowering cacti naturally occurring in Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. They live on other plants without harming them; one species, Rhipsalis baccifera, also occurs in Africa and Asia and is the only cactus naturally found in the Old World.
A genus of flowering plants native to the Cape Provinces of South Africa.
A genus of flowering plants native mostly to southern Africa, with four species reaching tropical Africa. Nearly all grow from corms, while one species grows from rhizomes.

A genus of evergreen flowering shrubs native to elevated grassland in South Africa, Lesotho and Namibia. They have large divided leaves and upright clusters of nectar-rich flowers. Their vegetative parts are very toxic.

A genus of bulb-growing perennial flowering plants native to southern Africa. Their leaves form rosettes at the base, while stout stems carry star-shaped flowers crowned with a green tuft, creating a pineapple-like appearance.
A genus of liverworts in the family Scapaniaceae.

A genus of flowering plants in the mallow family. Its flowers remain closed and attract many hummingbirds, while its red, fleshy fruit divides into five parts. The fruit is made into jelly or syrup, and both fruit and flowers are used for herbal teas.
edibilityNote: Fruit is made into jelly or syrup; fruit and flowers are used for herbal teas.

summary: A genus of tropical and warm-temperate annual and perennial flowering plants, mostly native to Central America and Mexico, with four species native to the United States. They bear fluffy lavender-blue, pink, lilac or white flowers in small clusters. Several species are toxic; A. houstonianum and A. conyzoides cause liver lesions and can promote tumors.

A deciduous flowering tree native to South America, specifically northern Argentina and Bolivia. It has a broad, dense crown and hard, winged pods with the seed at one end. Its aggressive roots can lift concrete and asphalt and damage nearby structures.

A genus of freshwater green algae with a widespread, cosmopolitan distribution. Its species form hollow spherical colonies containing hundreds to tens of thousands of coordinated cells, with different cells handling movement and reproduction. Colonies can reproduce sexually or asexually.

A genus of trees and large shrubs native to Australia and New Guinea. Some, but not all, have exceptionally stout trunks that store water during drought, and some shed their leaves in the dry season. Every species bears separate male and female flowers on the same plant.
A flowering-plant genus, Russelia includes species that grow in many parts of the world and are mildly drought resistant.

A genus of woody climbing vines distributed through tropical and subtropical Southeast Asia and Oceania. They climb using roots that emerge from their stems, and their leaves grow in three spirals. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, while the berries often form red cylindrical or rounded heads.

A moss genus, Leucobryum has species that form dense, upright, often rounded cushions ranging from white to bluish-green. Their thick, pale leaves are distinctive, and spore-producing structures are rare.

A genus of shrubs and trees occurring from Hawaii across the Pacific to tropical Asia, Australia and New Zealand. Its species have simple or three-part leaves, usually in opposite pairs, four-part flowers in branching clusters, and fruits divided into as many as four seed-bearing sections.

An annual legume most likely originating in the Near East, fenugreek has three small leaflets. Its leaves and seeds have been culinary ingredients since ancient times, and it has a distinctive maple-syrup smell.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten fresh or dried; seeds are used whole or ground and are often roasted to reduce their bitterness.

summary: A genus of legumes occurring naturally in the Canary Islands, southern Europe, non-tropical Africa, western and central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and Australia.

A tropical perennial thought native to southern India and Southeast Asia, taro grows from a starchy underground corm and bears large, heart-shaped leaves. Its corms and young leaves are eaten after thorough cooking; raw or undercooked taro is irritating and potentially toxic.
edibilityNote: Corms and young leaves are eaten after cooking; raw or undercooked taro can cause irritation and severe digestive problems.

summary: An annual legume cultivated for its edible seeds, the chickpea has small feathery leaves and white flowers with blue, violet or pink veins. Its protein-rich seeds are central to foods such as hummus, falafel, curries, soups and stews.
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten cooked, ground into flour or made into dishes such as hummus and falafel; young leaves are sometimes cooked as greens.

summary: A tropical herbaceous perennial native to South America, pineapple has tough, waxy leaves around a short stem. Its many individual flowers fuse into one crowned fruit, whose edible flesh and juice are used worldwide.
edibilityNote: The fruit's flesh and juice are consumed fresh, cooked, canned, fermented and in drinks, desserts and savoury dishes.

summary: A genus of bromeliad plants with a native range including tropical South America, Ananas includes Ananas comosus, the pineapple, and Ananas macrodontes, the false pineapple.

An herbaceous perennial originating in Asia, ginger grows annual leafy false stems and sends pale yellow, purple-edged flowers directly from its underground stem. This fragrant, pungent stem is widely used as a spice, including fresh, dried, pickled and candied forms.
edibilityNote: The underground stem is eaten or used as a spice fresh, dried, pickled or candied; leaves have also flavored food or been eaten.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native to China, the Indian subcontinent, New Guinea and Southeast Asia, Zingiber comprises the true gingers. Culinary uses differ by species: myoga is valued for its stems and flowers, while garden ginger supplies the familiar spice from its underground stem.
edibilityNote: Culinary uses vary by species; myoga stems and flowers are valued, while garden ginger's underground stem is used whole, candied, dried or powdered.

summary: A small to medium deciduous tree native to Iran and Central Asia, pistachio has separate male and female trees. Its edible elongated seed has pale green flesh inside a hard cream shell that often splits open with an audible pop when ripe.
edibilityNote: The seed is eaten fresh, roasted or salted, and used in desserts, confectionery, paste and butter; it is a priority allergen.

summary: An annual leaf vegetable native from the Mediterranean to Siberia, lettuce has leaves ranging from dense heads to loose, frilly forms in many colors. Leaves are usually eaten raw in salads, though they also appear in sandwiches, wraps and soups; some varieties provide edible stems or seeds pressed for cooking oil.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked and used in salads, sandwiches, wraps and soups; some varieties provide edible stems or seeds pressed for cooking oil.

summary: A tropical evergreen tree native to tropical South America, cashew bears a kidney-shaped true fruit at the end of a larger red or yellow cashew apple. The raw seed and its shell are toxic, but the seed is edible after shelling and roasting or steaming; the cashew apple is also eaten or made into drinks.
edibilityNote: The seed is edible after shelling and roasting or steaming; the cashew apple is eaten fresh or processed into drinks, preserves and other foods.

summary: A tropical evergreen tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Borneo, mangosteen bears fruit with a thick, deep reddish-purple inedible rind. Inside, fragrant white flesh surrounds the seeds and is sweet, tangy, juicy and edible; the picked fruit does not ripen further.
edibilityNote: The white inner flesh is eaten fresh, canned or frozen, served as dessert, or made into jam; the rind is inedible.

summary: A large evergreen fruit tree native to India and possibly the Western Ghats, jackfruit produces the largest tree-borne fruits, with a thick bumpy shell and many yellow fleshy bulbs, each enclosing a seed. The bulbs can be eaten raw, while the edible seeds are usually boiled or roasted; ripe fruit is sweet and unripe fruit is cooked in savory dishes.
edibilityNote: The bulbs can be eaten raw; seeds are usually boiled or roasted, ripe fruit is used in sweets, and unripe fruit in savory dishes.

summary: A genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution, Ceratodon belongs to the family Ditrichaceae and includes species such as C. purpureus and C. conicus.

A genus of evergreen shrubs native to the southwestern United States and Mexico, Leucophyllum has white-haired foliage and solitary bell- or funnel-shaped flowers ranging from white to magenta and purple. These salt-tolerant shrubs grow in sandy soils and often bloom several days before rain, apparently in response to humidity.
A globally distributed genus of mosses. Its members form dense clumps of packed upright stems that may fork but do not branch; in North America they are common in jack pine and red pine stands.

A worldwide genus of mosses, with most species occurring in the Southern Hemisphere. They commonly grow in tufts or mats on coastal trees, though some species grow on rocks, and their leaves characteristically curl when dry.

A palm native to southwestern South America and restricted to a small area of central Chile. It is among the most massive palms, with an exceptionally thick trunk. Its edible seeds are widely eaten as Coquito nuts, while its sap is made into wine or syrup by methods now restricted under legal protection.
edibilityNote: Seeds are widely eaten as Coquito nuts; sap makes palm wine and syrup, although harvesting it by felling trees is legally restricted.

summary: A slow-growing shrub or small tree thought to be native to the southeastern foothills of the Himalayas. Its large, fragrant fruit has a thick, coarse rind and usually dry pulp with little juice. The rind is commonly cooked in syrup or candied for sweets and cakes.
edibilityNote: The thick rind is cooked in syrup or candied; the fruit also supplies juice, drinks, preserves, pickles and seasonings.

summary: A genus of mosses with a worldwide distribution.

A fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree native to Macaronesia—the Azores, Madeira and Canary Islands. Its roots host bacteria that enable nitrogen fixation, and it has become invasive in Hawaii, Australia and New Zealand. The sweet, edible fruits are slightly astringent and can stain skin and the mouth blue.
edibilityNote: Sweet fruits are edible but little appreciated because they are astringent and roughen the tongue; they have also been made into wine.

summary: A genus of mostly compact perennial shrubs or vines, mainly native to tropical America but occurring throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. Its species range from delicate plants with paper-thin leaves to drought-tolerant forms with thick, waxy stems and leaves. Their usually inconspicuous flowers grow on cordlike spikes.
A genus of mosses with a worldwide distribution.
A genus of mosses found on every continent, including Antarctica, with its greatest diversity in the Northern Hemisphere.

A moss species classed as European, although its original range is unknown. It forms soft carpets with regularly feathered, swollen-looking shoots; branching may become irregular on disturbed ground such as mown lawns. Its leaves range from yellow-green to dark green and curve distinctly backward at the tip.
A genus of flowering plants native to temperate regions of the Old World. It includes 16 recognized species; one is caraway, whose seeds are widely used as a spice.
edibilityNote: Caraway, one member species, has seeds widely used as a spice; food use is not established for the genus as a whole.

summary: A genus of aromatic flowering herbs native to tropical and subtropical Asia, Australia and the Pacific Islands. They grow from thick underground stems and form apparent stems from overlapping leaf sheaths. Several species are ornamental, while some are used as spices, including galangal.
edibilityNote: Some species are used as spices, including galangal.

summary: A thorny citrus shrub or small tree native to tropical Southeast Asia. Its hourglass-like double leaves and small, bumpy fruit release an intense citrus fragrance; the fruit ripens from green to yellow and tastes very acidic and slightly bitter. The leaves flavor Southeast Asian dishes, while the rind is used in curry pastes and the whole fruit is candied in Cambodia.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used fresh, dried or frozen; rind flavors Lao and Thai curry pastes, and whole fruit is candied in Cambodia.

summary: A genus of submerged aquatic mosses widespread across the Northern Hemisphere. It has dark green, irregularly branching stems with glossy, sharply ridged leaves and commonly attaches to underwater rocks and logs in clean, acidic freshwater. These mosses provide habitat for stream invertebrates, fish eggs, algae and microorganisms.

A genus of freshwater filamentous algae that forms free-floating, yellow-green to bright green tangled mats. Each barrel-shaped cell bears two star-shaped chloroplasts, while young plants may anchor to streambeds. One terrestrial species, Z. terrestre, is known from India.

A cosmopolitan family of green algae whose members may be single-celled or form unbranched filaments. Their chloroplasts have varied shapes, including star-shaped in Zygnema, spiral in Spirogyra and flat in Mougeotia. They commonly form floating mats in still freshwater, though some attach to surfaces in moving water.

A genus of freshwater filamentous green algae found on every continent, including Antarctica. It is recognizable by spiral chloroplasts and free-floating, slimy filaments, each wrapped in a watery sheath. It can reproduce by fragmentation or by conjugation.

A genus of green algae common in freshwater worldwide. Each solitary cell has two matching halves and is typically long and crescent-shaped, with a transparent wall that may darken brown as iron and manganese accumulate. It usually clings to sediment or aquatic plants, though it can float freely or occur in wet soil.

A worldwide freshwater family of green algae whose members are single-celled or colonial. Their cells take varied shapes and may have smooth or ornamented walls. Some cell walls decay very slowly, allowing them to persist in the fossil record.
A large genus of liverworts found on every continent except Antarctica, with most species occurring in the tropics. Its species count remains under revision, with estimates ranging from 500 to 1,300.

A large genus of perennial spring flowers in the lily family, Gagea is found mainly in Eurasia, with a few species extending into North Africa and one into North America. Many appear briefly in early spring and retreat to underground bulbs by mid-spring or summer.
A genus of mosses, Aulacomnium has a circumpolar distribution.
A genus of about 30 flowering-plant species, Caralluma occurs in tropical Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Several taxa in the genus are valued as food.
edibilityNote: Several taxa are valued as food; C. adscendens has bitter, salty succulent branches eaten raw.

summary: A flowering-plant genus native to Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, Adenium is valued for colorful flowers and unusual swollen stem bases and is often grown as bonsai. The sap of A. boehmianum, A. multiflorum and A. obesum contains toxic cardiac glycosides and has been used as arrow poison in Africa.

A genus of perennial flowering plants native to Europe and western Asia, Pulmonaria has one species extending east to central Asia. Lungworts form hairy clumps or rosettes, often with prominently spotted leaves; flower buds commonly open pink or violet and mature to blue.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs native to eastern and southeastern Asia, especially China and Vietnam, Aspidistra grows in shade beneath trees and shrubs. Its leaves rise almost directly from underground stems, while its fleshy flowers usually appear low among the foliage near ground level.

A cultivated group of perennial deciduous shrub hybrids originating in China, Paeonia × suffruticosa is not a naturally occurring species. It has short, thick woody branches and reddish-purple, pink or white flowers that appear in May.

A genus of grasses occurring in Africa, Eurasia and the Pacific Islands, Miscanthus includes several species noted for great height and biomass production. Some are grown as ornamental grasses, and cold tolerance varies widely across the genus.

An herbaceous or semi-woody flowering perennial native to North America, Glandularia bipinnatifida ranges from the United States south to Nicaragua. It has finely divided leaves and pink or purple flowers, produced mainly in spring but potentially throughout the growing season.

A genus of small trees and large shrubs whose natural range is restricted to warm-temperate and tropical Asia, Photinia extends from the Himalayas to Japan and south through India, Indochina and Malesia. Most species are evergreen, often with glossy leaves, and bear small apple-shaped fruits that ripen in autumn and may persist into winter.
edibilityNote: Some varieties contain cyanogenic glycosides in foliage and fruit; chewing leaves releases hydrogen cyanide, but genus-wide human edibility is not established.

summary: A genus of perennial flowering plants from tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia, and Central and South America, with Africa considered its centre of origin. Begonias often have striking, asymmetrical leaves, while male and female flowers occur separately on the same plant.
edibilityNote: Some begonias are eaten in small amounts; their tissues contain oxalic acid, so large quantities may be toxic.

summary: A genus of fragrant, bulb-growing spring perennials native mainly from the eastern Mediterranean through Iraq and Iran to Turkmenistan. Each bulb produces narrow, untoothed leaves and one to three flower spikes; cultivated forms may have especially dense spikes.
edibilityNote: The bulbs are inedible and contain oxalic acid; handling them may also mildly irritate skin.

summary: A small genus of evergreen shrubs native to Korea, southern Japan and Taiwan. They have stout, sparsely branched stems and large, leathery, deeply lobed leaves, followed by creamy-white late-season flowers and small black fruit.

A genus of flowering plants native to tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia, Madagascar, Australia and the Pacific Islands. Most species are shrubs or small trees, and garden-grown species are remembered for large pale flowers with a strong, sweet scent that may intensify at night.

A genus of flowering shrubs and trees native across the tropics and subtropics, with a few species in warm-temperate Eurasia and one in New Zealand. Most have opposite leaves divided into several leaflets, fragrant branched flower spikes, and fleshy red, purple or black fruit.
A genus of mosses with a worldwide distribution, reported especially from tropical Asian countries. It is commonly called spike moss.

A genus of tropical and subtropical perennial herbs native to the Americas, with upright shoots arising from underground rhizomes. Different species are cultivated for food; Canna indica rhizomes are roasted or boiled like potatoes or milled into flour.
edibilityNote: Different Canna species are cultivated for food; C. indica rhizomes are roasted, boiled or milled into flour.

summary: A small genus of edible and ornamental flowering plants in the amaranth family. Its colourful, flame-like flower heads may develop the crested form called cockscomb; one documented member, Celosia argentea var. argentea, is cooked as a leafy vegetable.
edibilityNote: The genus is described as edible; C. argentea var. argentea leaves, young stems and young flower clusters are cooked in stews.

summary: A genus of mosses with 15 accepted species reported as of December 2014.

A genus of trees, shrubs and tropical woody vines native mainly to Africa, with other species from Asia and the American tropics and one distributed throughout the tropics. Entada produces exceptionally large pods, and its buoyant seeds can survive long journeys through rivers and ocean currents before washing onto beaches.

A small genus of ferns native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. They grow on other plants, spreading by creeping hairy or scaly stems, and bear their spore cases on the backs of evergreen fronds.

A deciduous shrub or tree native to East and Southeast Asia. Its rough, toothed leaves can be lobed or unlobed even on the same plant, while its inner bark is traditionally made into barkcloth and paper. The fruit and cooked leaves are edible.
edibilityNote: The fruit and cooked leaves are edible; the species has long been cultivated for food in Asia and some Pacific islands.

summary: A genus of red algae native to tropical through temperate coastal waters of all oceans. Its members may be upright or trailing, with flat or cylindrical branches arranged in two rows, rings or all directions; some appear iridescent.
edibilityNote: Humans have long used Laurencia as food, though no parts or preparation are specified.

summary: A genus of mosses; no native origin is supplied.

A genus of flowering perennials and subshrubs native to central and southern Europe, Macaronesia, northwestern Africa and southwestern Asia. They form dense, low evergreen mats with leathery oval leaves and tightly packed heads of purple, violet, pink or white flowers.
A genus of herbs and shrubs native across Mexico and North, Central and South America. Its members have finely divided leaves that fold in the evening and are commonly called bundleflowers.

A genus of flowering perennial herbs and subshrubs; no native origin is explicitly supplied. Their usually hairy foliage accompanies flower heads whose rays are yellowish above but may be green, red, maroon or dark-veined beneath.

A genus of mostly tree- or rock-growing orchids with an evolutionary origin in the Asia-Pacific and a pantropical range. Creeping roots spread over trees or rocks, and the stems usually bear a swollen section topped by one leaf. Many species produce carrion-like odours that attract pollinating flies, although others are pleasantly scented.

A genus of evergreen orchids native from tropical and subtropical Asia to Australia. Its members may grow on trees, rocks or soil, and usually bear long-lived leaves on swollen stems. Their unbranched flower stalks arise from the stem base, with a distinctive three-lobed central petal.

A genus of flowering vines and shrubs native to tropical and subtropical sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, southern Asia, New Guinea and Australia. Its members are vigorous annuals or perennials, and some escape from gardens and become invasive.
A genus of flowering plants native to South Africa's Cape Provinces.
A genus of herbaceous perennial flowering plants native to Europe, North Africa, Western and Central Asia, and Siberia.

A North American herbaceous perennial found mainly in the east-central United States, with isolated populations farther west and north. It has wiry stems, spreads through underground stems, and produces abundant clusters of bright yellow flowers from midsummer to fall.

A genus of long-lived, rosette-forming succulent plants native mainly to mountainous, arid Mexico, with some species also native to the southwestern United States. Numerous evergreen leaves persist after dying, often forming a skirt around the trunk. Historically, the crowns were baked or roasted and made into flour, while flowering stems were eaten raw, boiled or roasted.
edibilityNote: Historically, crowns were baked or roasted, dried and pounded into flour for cakes; flowering stems were eaten raw, boiled or roasted.

summary: A flowering-plant genus represented by one circumboreal succulent perennial found along northern temperate and Arctic coasts. Its only species forms spreading patches above the high-water mark, with branching stems buried in sand and fleshy paired leaves.

A genus of flowering plants native to New Zealand, Australia and South Africa's Cape Provinces. Its members are low-growing annuals or short-lived succulent shrubs whose branches root at the joints, with fleshy leaves and daisy-like flowers usually borne singly at shoot tips.

A one-species genus of coniferous trees native to northeastern East Asia and North Asia. Its sole species has flattened sprays of scale-like foliage that may turn brownish, yellow-green or coppery orange in winter, and pale-green cones that ripen to brown.

A genus of herbs, shrubs and climbing plants native to South America, including Chile and Peru, and ranging from Patagonia to central Mexico. Its flowers are usually yellow or orange and may be spotted red or purple.
A moss genus with an almost cosmopolitan distribution.
A genus of flowering plants native to the American tropics. Some species have colourful foliage and are grown as ornamentals, while the flowers are covered in fine hairs.

A genus of red algae found worldwide from tropical to temperate waters. Its upright, branching bodies alternate between calcified and uncalcified sections and grow attached to reef surfaces from intertidal to subtidal areas.
edibilityNote: Species are described as unpalatable because they are highly calcified, but not explicitly inedible.

summary: A worldwide family of red algae. Every member has a chalky, calcified outer layer.

A genus of red algae found from Arctic and temperate waters to the tropics. Its low, crust-like bodies attach to surfaces and may be partly or fully calcified with aragonite crystals. Members occur from intertidal shores to deep water, including records at 288 metres in the Bahamas.

A worldwide genus of red seaweeds with hard, branching, calcareous skeletons. Its upright forked branches alternate between red or pink calcified sections and white uncalcified joints, while small creeping holdfasts anchor it to surfaces.
A family of freshwater and marine red algae comprising about 100 genera.
A genus of red algae. Griffithsin is a protein isolated from species in this genus.
A worldwide genus of red algae. Its bodies form repeatedly forked branches with a filament-built inner tissue.

A genus of flowering herbs and small shrubs found throughout the tropics and subtropics, with greatest diversity in the Americas. Its four-lobed flowers form compact heads and range from white to blue, pink or maroon; some species have strikingly coloured outer flower parts.
A tribe of woody bamboos from tropical regions, including some giant forms. It is the most diverse bamboo tribe and divides into major New World and Old World tropical lineages.

A genus of annuals, shrubs and subshrubs native to scrub and dry grassland from the southwestern United States to South America, with greatest diversity in Mexico. Their long-stemmed flower heads range from single rows to domed forms and occur in many bright colours. Some zinnias are edible, though often bitter and mainly suited to garnish.
edibilityNote: Some zinnias are edible but often bitter and best suited to garnish.

summary: A genus of coarse annual or perennial herbs and shrubs centred in Mexico and native also to Central America; one species reaches the southwestern United States, and another is a small tree. Its distinctive flower stalk is hollow and flares near the top. T. diversifolia and T. rotundifolia are widely cultivated and have escaped as tropical and subtropical weeds.
A genus of flowering plants in which one species is native to tropical Africa and southern India, while the others are endemic to southern and eastern Africa.

A genus of evergreen shrubs and small trees with a pan-tropical distribution across Africa, Asia, Australia, the Americas and Indian and Pacific islands. They have opposite leaves with milky sap and fragrant white flowers.
A genus of flowering plants native to tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

A genus of mostly evergreen shrubs and trees, with rare vines, naturally distributed from tropical Africa through Southeast Asia and Australia to Pacific islands. Its leaves vary greatly, from undivided to repeatedly divided, while its flower clusters may be upright or hanging and take several forms.

A genus of tropical trees native to Africa, Asia, Australasia and islands of the Indian and Pacific oceans. Many species have unusually large leaves, and the plants are noted as pioneers. Their hollow stems often house ants that attack plant-eating insects.

A genus of evergreen shrubs and trees distributed through tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and the Americas. Its usually solitary flowers are followed by fleshy, berry-like capsules that may open to reveal dangling seeds with a fleshy red coating.

A genus of herbs, subshrubs and shrubs native from the Mediterranean east through central Asia to China. The plants are often hairy, with opposite leaf pairs set at right angles and flowers arranged in whorls around usually square stems.

A single-stemmed palm native to a very small area of northeastern Queensland, Australia. Its many finely divided leaflets radiate around each frond, creating a bushy foxtail appearance, and its ripe fruit is orange-red with one large seed.
A genus of two palms endemic to Lord Howe Island, Australia. Both are spineless, moderate-sized palms with upright bare trunks marked by prominent leaf scars and feather-like leaves.

A slow-growing, long-lived evergreen conifer native to southern South America and endemic to temperate rainforests of southern Chile and adjacent Argentina. Its dark purple-brown bark flakes or scales, while its hard, prickly-tipped leaves have two blue-white bands underneath.

A small, slow-growing conifer native to northwestern Africa's Atlas Mountains, with small outlying populations on Malta and near Cartagena in Spain. It can resprout from stumps after wildfire or browsing, and repeated regrowth produces large burls at the trunk base.
An evergreen conifer endemic to Japan. Its red-brown bark peels in vertical strips, and its thick, almost fleshy scale-like leaves are glossy green above with vivid white bands underneath.

An evergreen conifer native to the Appalachian Mountains of the southeastern United States. Its flexible needles have a strong turpentine-like fragrance, while its upright dark-purple cones turn brown and break apart when mature to release winged seeds.

A fern found in wet forests across Australia except Western Australia. It has distinctly different fertile and sterile fronds, and its underground stems can spread over a great distance before sending up new fronds.
A genus of 22 flowering legume species ranging from Arizona through Mexico and Central America to Colombia and Venezuela.

A perennial legume native to the Eastern Hemisphere, although its precise geographical origin is debated; India is considered its primary centre and West Africa a second major centre. It is notably drought-resistant, and its peas are eaten dried, ground into flour or as green vegetables.
edibilityNote: Dried peas, flour and green peas are foods; dried peas may also be briefly sprouted and then cooked.

summary: A genus of orchids occurring in humid low- to mid-elevation forests of South America, with most species in Brazil. Most grow on other plants, though some grow on the ground, and they bear fragrant, waxy, long-lived flowers in varied green, purple, burgundy and raspberry patterns.

An orchid genus distributed from India and the Himalayas through Southeast Asia and southern China to New Guinea and northern Australia. Most grow on trees, often becoming massive, with leathery, drought-resistant leaves and large aerial root systems; their showy, fragrant, intensely colourful flowers are prized in horticulture.

An orchid genus native to Mexico, Central America, the West Indies and South America. Its small but sturdy plants mostly grow on trees in shady forests, bearing short, arching or hanging sprays of showy, fragrant flowers.

An orchid genus native to Asia, New Guinea and Australia. Moth orchids usually grow on trees, with coarse roots, short leafy stems, large leathery leaves and long-lasting, flat flowers on upright or hanging sprays.

An orchid genus native to Mexico, Central America, the West Indies and northern South America, with B. caudata extending into Florida. These wet-forest plants have long, spreading floral parts resembling spiders; female spider-hunter wasps mistake the flowers for prey and pollinate them while attacking.

A bromeliad genus found mainly from Cuba and Mexico south to Argentina, especially in Colombia, Peru and Brazil; P. feliciana is the tropical West African exception. Almost all grow on the ground or rocks in moist areas, although many also grow on trees.

A genus of mainly stemless, evergreen bromeliads native to Brazil, southern Mexico, Central America, and northern and western South America. Most grow on other plants, and the parent dies after flowering while new plants develop from offsets.

A bromeliad genus widespread across Latin America and the West Indies. Its flowers have a deeply split outer cup; fibres from B. serra and B. hieronymi are economically important to the Wichí people of Argentina’s semi-arid Gran Chaco.

A genus of small palms native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. They grow beneath rainforest canopies on slender, cane-like stems and often spread underground into colonies; male and female flowers occur on separate plants.

A genus of evergreen flowering perennials native to tropical Asia and China. They form clumps of mainly heart- or arrow-shaped leaves, often smell strongly of anise, and hide tiny petal-free flowers inside a usually green sheath beneath the foliage.

A genus of aquatic plants naturally distributed across tropical India, Southeast Asia and New Guinea. Water trumpets inhabit slow-moving lowland forest streams and rivers, seasonally flooded pools and riverbanks; their flower spike is enclosed by a trumpet-shaped sheath.

Flowering-plant genus native to South and Central America, where it grows in forest openings and along riverbanks and goes dormant during the dry season. Several species are ornamentals with large, arrowhead-shaped leaves patterned in white, pink and red; all parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous and should not be ingested.

summary: Evergreen flowering-plant genus native to tropical and subtropical Asia and New Guinea, especially humid, shady forests. Wild species often have broad, silver-and-green variegated leaves, and ripe fruits are red berries; the plants are poisonous if ingested.
edibilityNote: The plants are poisonous; ingestion irritates the mucous membranes.

summary: Flowering-plant genus of medicinal and ornamental chaff flowers; no native origin is supplied. Its members are characterized by solitary fertile flowers.

Bromeliad genus native to Latin America from Mexico to Chile, including mountainous regions. Unlike other bromeliads, Greigia plants do not die after flowering; the same rosette blooms again each year.

Evergreen, rosette-forming bromeliad genus native to forests and scrub in southern Mexico, the West Indies, Central America and South America. Most species grow on other plants, and their leaf funnels collect water; flowers are often brilliantly coloured, and their petals curl as they wither.
Fern genus with no native origin supplied. Its leaflets bear round reproductive clusters underneath rather than separate reproductive fronds, and the frond stalks often have prominent scales.
Evergreen flowering-plant genus native to Central and South America, primarily Brazil. It is grown for attractive, often variegated foliage and is frost-tender.

Orchid genus native to South America. Its plants may carry arching sprays crowded with small pale green, cream, yellowish or white flowers, sometimes streaked red; many species are difficult to distinguish except by flower structure.

Bamboo genus native to China and Japan. It spreads vigorously through shallow underground stems that produce plantlets at their joints and can become invasive if not removed; P. variegatus has green-and-cream stripes, while P. viridistriatus has green-and-yellow stripes.

A coniferous shrub or small tree native to China, the Korean Peninsula, Japan and Taiwan. Its leathery, yellowish-green leaves rise in two ranks to form a narrow V, with two pale silvery bands beneath. Male and female cones grow on separate plants.
A genus of plants in the daisy family, Ozothamnus is found in Australia, New Zealand and New Caledonia.

A tall, grain-bearing perennial tropical grass native to Southeast Asia. Its wild variety has very hard, pearly white oval cases used as beads, while cultivated variety ma-yuen has soft shells and is harvested as a cereal. Across East Asia, dried grains are cooked and widely eaten, especially in gruels.
edibilityNote: Dried grains, especially from soft-shelled cultivated varieties, are cooked across East Asia as cereal or gruel.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to south-central China and Tibet, common buckwheat has red stems, arrow-shaped leaves and pink-and-white flowers. Its sharply three-angled, starchy seeds are eaten like cereal even though the plant is not a grass; buckwheat can trigger severe allergies.
edibilityNote: The hulled, starchy seeds are eaten as groats or flour in foods such as porridge and noodles; severe allergic reactions are reported.

summary: A monotypic genus of bean-family plants, Lablab contains only Lablab purpureus.

A genus of six flowering-tree species native to Mexico, the Caribbean, Central America and northern South America. These moderate-sized trees bear large spherical fruits with thin, hard shells and soft pulp; the shells are used for containers, scoops and cups.

A genus of perennial tropical herbs native to the New World tropics from Mexico and the West Indies south to Argentina. Straight stems carry alternate leaves patterned with white spots and flecks, and many species tolerate shade as houseplants. Chewing the leaves exposes needle-shaped crystals that can cause oral burning, numbness and swelling, sometimes temporarily preventing speech.
edibilityNote: Chewing or ingesting leaves exposes needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals, causing oral burning, numbness, drooling and swelling; severe throat exposure may impede breathing.

summary: A genus of flowering plants native to Australia.

A genus of herbs and small shrubs with about 110 species in Australia and 36 in New Zealand. Leaves are usually opposite and paler underneath, while branch-tip flower clusters lack petals but have four petal-like sepals. The fruit is usually a one-seeded nut.

A genus of epiphytic herbs and shrubs native to the tropical Americas and Caribbean. Its usually large, brightly coloured flowers are tubular or oddly shaped, often red, yellow or orange, and can resemble fish.
A moss genus with a cosmopolitan distribution.
An order of multicellular red algae, Ahnfeltiales contains just one family, Ahnfeltiaceae.
A shrub endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands, where it grows in laurel forests, generally at higher elevations. Its terminal flower clusters open white and later turn lilac.
A genus of deciduous shrubs native to eastern Asia. Its pointed, serrated leaves accompany clusters of five-lobed flowers that appear in early summer and are white, pink or red, and rarely yellow.

A family of freshwater green algae found worldwide, with some members also living in brackish water. Their brittle stems may become coated in lime and smell foul when stepped on, while whorls of small branches give them a horsetail-like appearance.

A genus of flowering succulents native to semi-desert areas of Central America, Mexico and northwestern South America. These evergreen plants form compact rosettes of fleshy, often brightly coloured leaves, produce flowers repeatedly during their lives and commonly develop numerous offsets.
A genus of liverworts found in the Northern Hemisphere. Species may be green, brownish or reddish, with smooth-edged, unlobed leaves and narrow, tapered underleaves; some plants also bear gemmae.
A genus of plants in the mint family, native to North and South America.

A genus of tropical trees distributed from Mexico through Central and South America to Bolivia and southern Brazil, and in the Caribbean. Its trees have hand-shaped clusters of leaflets and oval, woody fruits that split open to release many seeds.

A genus of flowering shrubs native to China, Taiwan and Vietnam. Warm-climate species are evergreen, while colder-climate species are deciduous; their usually scented, bell-shaped flowers range from white to pink and bloom from late spring into autumn.
A genus of mosses found worldwide.
A genus of mosses with no native range supplied. It contained 91 species as of July 2021.
A genus of grasses from Eurasia and Africa.
A genus of mosses found worldwide in both hemispheres. Its small to medium plants form dense mats or cushions, with leaves held upright when moist and crinkled when dry.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs native to the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and China. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, and one species, Thladiantha cordifolia, has nectar glands outside its flowers.
A genus of flowering plants native to the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, southern China and Malesia. It comprises five accepted species.

A genus of flowering herbs and low shrubs abundant around the Mediterranean, the Balkans, Iberian Peninsula and Macaronesia, and also found in Central Europe and temperate Asia. They are generally short and hairy, often growing at high elevations on rocks with little soil. Several named species and other members of section Empedoclia are boiled as herbal tea using stems, leaves and flowers.
edibilityNote: Several named species and other members of section Empedoclia are boiled as tea using stems, leaves and flowers, often served with honey and lemon.

summary: A mat-forming genus found on every continent except Antarctica. It typically has creeping, irregularly branched shoots and enlarged, inflated, often coloured cells at the leaf bases.

A genus of cacti found in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. They climb or grow on trees, rocks or the ground, producing aerial roots and large flowers that open at night. Several species produce edible pitaya or dragon fruit, gathered from the wild or cultivated.
edibilityNote: Fruits of several species are eaten; some are gathered wild, while others are cultivated as pitaya or dragon fruit.

summary: A genus of mosses in the family Pottiaceae.

A genus of small, delicate rock mosses growing as dark brown or reddish cushions on wet, silica-rich rocks in mountainous areas. Their spore capsules lack the usual lid and teeth, opening along four vertical slits while remaining joined at both ends.

A genus of tropical plants ranging from short shrubs to tall upright forms, native to tropical Africa, southern and eastern Asia, Australia and various oceanic islands. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Its fleshy, juicy fruits are edible and change from white through red to black as they ripen.
edibilityNote: Fleshy, juicy fruits are edible and taste sour to bittersweet; some people find Antidesma bunius berries bitter.

summary: A genus of evergreen, rhizomatous flowering perennials native to Africa, including Madagascar. Its mostly blue, star-shaped flowers generally last only a morning, while clusters open in sequence over several weeks.

A family of tiny liverworts that recent molecular studies treat as containing only Arnellia fennica. Its overlapping, opposite leaf-like structures are joined at the back of their bases; underleaves are absent and root-like rhizoids are rare.
A genus of mosses in the family Grimmiaceae.

A genus of shrubs and small trees native to southern and eastern Asia and northeastern Africa. Its small green leaves contrast with a leathery, multicoloured trunk, while the flowers are small and inconspicuous.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible but not an important crop; leaves are sometimes used as a tea substitute in China.

summary: A genus of large herbs and subshrubs native to the southwestern United States, Mexico and Central America; some members are naturalized elsewhere. It belongs to the groundsel tribe of the sunflower family.
A genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution, belonging to the Bryaceae family.

A cosmopolitan genus of mosses that grows on damp to wet silicate rock. Its lance-like leaves have browned bases and distinctive swollen orange-brown cells at their lower corners; its oval to pear-shaped spore capsules may lack teeth.
A genus of mosses in the Pottiaceae family with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A genus of mosses in the Pottiaceae family with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A genus of flowering plants native to North and South America, belonging to the sunflower family.

A genus of fan palms found on tropical Pacific islands, including Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, the Tuamotus and especially Hawaii. They have fan-shaped leaves and column-like trunks, with flowers and fruit borne in arching or hanging terminal clusters. Native Hawaiians often eat their seeds raw.
edibilityNote: Native Hawaiians often consume the palms' seeds, called hāwane or wāhane, raw.

summary: A genus of mosses found in Eurasia and northern North America.
A North American genus of plants in the aster family. Its species are commonly known as silkgrasses, golden asters or grass-leaved goldenasters.

An arum-family plant genus native to East Asia—China, Korea and Japan. Its green, hooded flower structure bears a long tongue-like projection, inspiring the common name green dragons. Leaves range from simple and heart-shaped to divided into several leaflets, and many species form small bulbs on their leaves.

A cactus genus native to the Neotropics. Its species are column-shaped shrubs or trees, sometimes densely branched; their usually night-opening flowers may smell strongly of garlic. Ripe fruits can have white, red-purple or other-coloured pulp.
A genus of deciduous trees native to eastern and northeastern Asia. They have leathery, feather-like leaves and clustered yellow flowers; some, but not all, species develop thick corky bark.
A genus of evergreen flowering vines native to the tropical Americas, from Florida and northeastern Mexico south to Bolivia, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
A genus of plants native to Europe, Asia and Africa.

A genus of flowering plants in the sunflower family, native to southern and northwestern Africa, Chad, Somalia and the southern Arabian Peninsula. One member, Pentzia incana, is naturalized in Australia and the southwestern United States.
A genus of large cacti native to Central America and Mexico. They form massive shrubs or small trees with stout stems; one member, Pachycereus pringlei, is the tallest recorded cactus species.
A genus of flowering plants native to Europe and western Asia. They produce blue or white, forget-me-not-like flowers in spring, and their seeds have a distinctive navel-like shape.

A genus of creeping, mat-forming perennial herbs native mainly to Southern Hemisphere parts of South America and Australasia, although one species extends into the Northern Hemisphere. Its flowers are inconspicuous, while the fruit is usually a bright orange berry but may be a dry capsule in some species.
A genus of flowering plants in the myrtle family, native to Central and South America, the West Indies and southern Florida.
A genus of flowering plants in the cabbage family, with three accepted species ranging from the Mediterranean through central and Eastern Europe and Western Asia to Siberia and northern China.

A one-species genus of flowering plants native to China and Korea. Its sole species is an annual or biennial with an upright, mostly unbranched stem and a large solitary flower head. Wild flowers are purple, while cultivated varieties offer many colours and single or double heads.
